meta.title: Five Boro Bike Tour - 2026

projection.description: GPS latitude/longitude was converted to a flat local (x, y) grid in miles using an equirectangular approximation, valid over this route's small (<0.2 degree) span: x = (lon - originLon) * milesPerDegreeLongitude, y = (lat - originLat) * milesPerDegreeLatitude. This global grid is only used to build each segment's own rotated coordinate frame -- see each segment's `frame` field for the coordinates actually used in its equation.

meta.segmentation: Segments were found with a greedy incremental line/curve extraction over the route's GPS track (similar in spirit to iterative end-point fit / Douglas-Peucker line simplification): starting from a point, we extend a candidate 'straight' run as far as possible while its maximum sideways deviation from the straight chord connecting its two ends stays under a small tolerance (0.6% of the run's length); if a run can't even start straight, we instead extend a candidate 'curve' run as far as a quadratic fit keeps explaining at least 93% of its sideways variation (R-squared). Whichever succeeds becomes one segment, and the process repeats from where it left off. This makes 'straight vs. curved' a property of the road's actual geometry, not an arbitrary grid.

hitDetection.description: For fast pointer/CV hit-testing on a <canvas>, render the route on an offscreen canvas where each GPS point (or small point-run) is drawn with its own flat, unique color, then read the pixel color under the cursor to recover which point id was hit -- a standard canvas 'color picking' technique (canvases have no native per-shape hit regions).
hitDetection.idField: point.id (0-based index into the `points` array) and segment.index
hitDetection.colorEncoding: hitColor = '#' + hex(( (id+1) >> 16) & 255) + hex(((id+1) >> 8) & 255) + hex((id+1) & 255), zero-padded to 2 hex digits each. id+1 reserves pure black (0) for 'no hit / background'.

legend.linear: Straight sections: the bike travels in one direction with (nearly) zero sideways drift -- a linear function y = mx + b.
legend.quadratic: Curved sections: the road bends steadily in one direction -- modeled with a quadratic y = ax^2 + bx + c.

frame.note: x runs along the segment's own direction of travel (rotationDeg, compass bearing); y is the perpendicular sideways offset from that direction, in miles. Origin is the segment's own starting point, so (x=0, y=0) is always the segment start.

segments.explanation: Segment 0 runs from mile 0.00 to mile 0.40 of the route (76 recorded GPS points) and was flagged as a broad curve because the road's heading keeps changing steadily rather than holding constant. We projected its GPS points into local x-y miles and rotated the frame to point along the chord from the segment's start to its end (compass heading 4°, N), with the origin at (40.71820°, -74.00544°). A least-squares quadratic regression of sideways position y against distance-traveled x then gives y = -0.1916x² + 0.1084x - 0.0073. The leading coefficient a = -0.1916 controls how sharply the road bends — its size reflects the tightness of the curve, and its sign (negative) tells us the road bows to the left of the straight-line chord. The vertex of this parabola falls at x = 0.283 miles into the segment — the point of sharpest turning — which lies inside this stretch, confirming the bend is centered here rather than at either end. The linear term b = 0.1084 reflects the road's initial direction relative to that chord, and the constant c = -0.0073 is forced near 0 by our choice of origin. This quadratic model explains about 49% of the sideways variation in the path (R² = 0.49), with roughly 29 feet of typical deviation — the remaining gap is real road geometry a single parabola can't fully capture, such as a compound curve or a brief straight tangent within the bend.

segments.explanation: Segment 1 runs from mile 0.40 to mile 0.76 of the route (57 recorded GPS points). To build its equation we took every GPS point in this stretch, converted latitude/longitude into flat x-y coordinates measured in miles (a small-area map projection centered near the start of the whole route), then rotated that coordinate grid so a new x-axis points along this segment's own direction of travel: compass heading 18° (NNE), starting from the GPS point at (40.72397°, -74.00473°). In that rotated frame we ran a least-squares linear regression of sideways position y against distance-traveled x, giving y = 0.0016x + 0.0007 (x and y in miles from the segment's start). The slope m = 0.0016 means the path drifts about 8.5 feet left of straight-ahead for every mile ridden — close to zero is a hallmark of a straight road. The intercept b = 0.0007 is forced close to 0 because we chose the x-axis to pass exactly through the segment's starting point. The actual GPS track wanders from this line by only about 4.9 feet on average (root-mean-square deviation) — roughly the size of normal GPS measurement error — which is exactly what we'd expect on a genuinely straight stretch of road.
